TOKYO, Nov 4 : Japan Investment Corp (JIC), a state-backed fund, plans to sell chipmaking materials maker JSR to Mitsui Chemicals in a deal that could exceed 1.3 trillion yen ($8.20 billion), two people familiar with the matter said. A decision could come as soon as within the month, one of the people said. Both people declined to be identified as the information is not public. JIC, JSR and Mitsui Chemicals did not reply to a request for comment. Shares in Mitsui Chemicals fell 7 per cent following Reuters' report. Reuters, which previously reported JIC is considering selling JSR, is reporting the final buyer for the first time.

JIC acquired JSR for some 900 billion yen two years ago and had said it planned to use the business to drive consolidation in the semiconductor materials sector. The fund will instead sell JSR to a domestic chemical major as it takes advantage of a lift in the valuation of chip-related firms due to a boom in AI investment. JSR, established in 1957, is a leading manufacturer of photoresists which are used to transfer circuit patterns onto semiconductor wafers. Mitsui Chemicals, which is also expanding its chip materials business, has a market capitalisation of about 800 billion yen. The deal could be among the largest in Japan's chemicals sector, exceeding the 2020 acquisition of Hitachi Chemical by Showa Denko which created Resonac Holdings. Mitsui Chemicals had 217.8 billion yen in cash and cash equivalents and 876.4 billion yen in interest-bearing debt as at the end of June. Its debt-to-equity ratio, a measure of financial soundness, stood at 0.75. JIC, which is overseen by the trade ministry, was set up in 2018 to invest in companies with the goal of boosting Japan's competitiveness. Its investments include medical equipment maker Topcon alongside private equity firm KKR. ($1 = 158.5200 yen)

Source: Reuters

Nov 3 : Block on Tuesday raised its full-year gross profit outlook after strength in its Cash App unit lifted the firm's quarterly earnings, while also reaching a preliminary settlement with the US Department of Justice over its anti-money laundering program. Shares of the Jack Dorsey-led company rose 7 per cent in extended trading. The US economy grew at its fastest pace in a year in the third quarter, shrugging off higher oil prices due to the Iran war, signaling that consumers maintained robust spending, benefiting financial firms such as Block. Gross profit at Cash App, Block's consumer-focused financial platform, surged 27 per cent in the third quarter from a year earlier. Gross profit at its Square merchant business rose 14 per cent.

Cash App's growing banking and lending products have helped Block diversify its revenue streams beyond transaction fees. "We've seen continued strong spending on Cash App Card as well as strong repayment rates on Borrow, which for us are the signals that collectively tell us consumers are managing their finances and the strength of their pocketbook," Chief Financial Officer Amrita Ahuja told Reuters in an interview. But the diversification has also increased the company's credit losses. Block's losses on transaction, loan and consumer receivables rose 65.6 per cent to $601.7 million in the third quarter. Block now expects gross profit of $12.63 billion for 2026, representing 22 per cent growth, compared with its prior forecast of $12.51 billion. It forecast gross profit of $3.32 billion for the fourth quarter. The fintech firm also forecast 2027 gross profit of $14.52 billion, implying 15 per cent growth, as it expects AI investments to drive sustained growth. Executive Officer and Head of Business Owen Jennings said the company expects the fourth quarter to mark the first time it generates revenue directly from AI tools. Adjusted operating income rose to $923 million, or $1.13 per share, for the three months ended September 30, compared with $480 million, or 54 cents per share, a year earlier. REGULATORY OVERHANG EASES Separately, Block said it reached an agreement in principle with the US Department of Justice in October to defer for three years a charge that the company failed to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program in violation of the Bank Secrecy Act. The deferred prosecution agreement could result in an expected net payment of roughly $764 million after credits for prior regulatory resolutions, the company added. The disclosure removes some uncertainty related to the probe but the DOJ resolution remains subject to a final agreement and court approval, and Block warned the ultimate terms could result in losses exceeding the amount already accrued.

Source: Reuters

Nov 3 : Meta Platforms said on Tuesday it is raising $15 billion through a five-part US dollar bond offering, as the Facebook parent turns to debt markets to help finance accelerating investments in AI infrastructure. The offering adds to a wave of AI-related fundraising as companies seek capital for data centers, computing capacity and cloud expansion, despite historically relying on strong cash balances to fund growth. It comprises $3.25 billion of notes due in 2031 carrying a 5.85 per cent coupon and another $3.25 billion due in 2033 at 6.25 per cent, according to a regulatory filing. Meta previously tapped debt markets with a $25 billion investment-grade bond sale in April and a $30 billion offering last year, underscoring its growing use of external financing to fund long-term AI investments.

Nov 3 : Booking Holdings said on Tuesday it recorded a $900 million reduction in revenue and accrued a loss of $100 million related to an FTC action involving Priceline's connection to deceptive hotel ads. The company warned that its business could face further fines after the online travel agency's third-quarter revenue fell 1 per cent year-over-year as a result. Shares of the company were down 1.5 per cent in extended trading. The FTC has been investigating Priceline's relationship with Guest Reservations, a third-party website which often charges higher prices and fees for hotel rooms, and whether it violates a rule against impersonating other businesses, and other potential violations regarding fees. Guest Reservations has been the subject of more than 1,000 consumers' complaints to the Better Business Bureau, many of whom said they believed they were booking directly with hotels. Consumers complained of surprise fees and unresponsive customer service representatives.

Priceline, which is one of Bookings five consumer facing brands, supplies hotel room inventory to Guest Reservations through Priceline Partner Solutions, according to an ongoing lawsuit against the companies filed by San Francisco. In addition to the $1 billion cumulative hit related to the matter, a settlement has not been agreed and litigation remains possible, the company said in a filling. A settlement "would likely" include an agreement for Priceline to pay a certain amount to the FTC directly as well as to provide monetary restitution to certain US consumers, the company said. The company warned that future litigation and regulatory processes in other jurisdictions related to similar claims, could harm the company's business, results and reputation. An FTC spokesperson declined to comment. The company said it is in discussions with the FTC to resolve the matter. Reuters reported in October that the case could carry more than $500 million in potential penalties. The charge comes as global travel demand moderated toward the end of the third quarter, reflecting softer international travel trends, while domestic travel has remained resilient, Booking said in a statement on Tuesday. Travel disruptions to and from the Middle East and elevated airfares due to the conflict affected demand in October, alongside localized unrest in certain European cities. However, gross bookings grew 10 per cent year-on-year during the quarter and room nights grew 7 per cent, as the travel industry has been supported by affluent travelers. The Norwalk, Connecticut-based company posted a profit per share of $4.66 for the third quarter, compared with $3.98 per share in the year-ago period. Analysts were expecting $4.50 per share, according to data compiled by LSEG. Total revenue for the quarter ended September 30 came in at $8.89 billion, compared to about $9 billion a year earlier.

Source: Reuters

Nov 3 : AMD forecast faster-than-expected 2027 growth as its data-center sales surge and its multibillion-dollar challenge to Nvidia gathers pace, sending its shares up 8 per cent in extended trading. The forecast and market-beating third-quarter results offered a strong counterpoint on Tuesday to mounting fears that the AI boom is losing steam and soothed investor concerns after rival Intel issued a weak outlook last week. Intel's shares rose 2 per cent, Nvidia stock climbed over 1 per cent and Broadcom also advanced 1.2 per cent. On a conference call with analysts, AMD CEO Lisa Su said the company expects overall revenue to rise more than 80 per cent in 2027. Su's forecast is higher than the 77 per cent growth analysts estimate, according to LSEG data.

Su told analysts that 80 per cent of sales next year will come from data-center chips that will "drive the majority of our revenue and earnings growth." "We see demand across the data-center business, across our CPU business, as well as our data-center AI business," Su said. "And when you look at the rate and pace of that growth, we've been planning for it for the last several years." Data-center revenue jumped 97 per cent to a record $8.55 billion in the third quarter, exceeding estimates of $8.20 billion. The company expects fourth-quarter revenue of about $17 billion, plus or minus 3 per cent, above analysts' average estimate of $16.23 billion, according to data compiled by LSEG. AMD's line of chips is positioned to benefit from the massive AI data-center buildout, portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds Hendi Susanto said. "The stock's resilience despite broader pressure on AI-related names suggests investors see AMD's results as confirming its technology leadership and its strong position to keep gaining market share," he added. AMD is benefiting as a shift in AI workloads toward running models in real-world applications drives demand for its graphics processing units and central processors. "The AMD numbers provide a greatly needed boost both for AI infrastructure and even, to a smaller degree, the PC market," chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research Bob O'Donnell said. The company's adjusted gross margin is expected to be about 55 per cent, in line with estimates of 55.27 per cent and down from 56 per cent in the third quarter. RAMPING UP AI ROLLOUTS AMD has stepped up AI product rollouts, moving beyond standalone chips to compete with Nvidia's rack-scale systems. The company's flagship Helios rack, combining its MI455X accelerator and new "Venice" server chips, is in production and set for a larger ramp-up in the fourth quarter. The initial systems are being tested at Meta. AMD's third-quarter revenue rose 45 per cent to $13.38 billion, beating estimates of $13.09 billion. Adjusted profit came in at $2.09 per share, compared with estimates of $1.95. The semiconductor industry is also grappling with a global memory shortage, leaving expensive high-bandwidth memory used in AI processors in scarce supply as manufacturers race to increase production. Third-quarter sales in AMD's client and gaming segment, home to its PC chips and console processors, fell 8 per cent to $3.72 billion, missing estimates of $3.79 billion. AMD said it expects PC unit shipments to decline by a double-digit percentage next year, though Su said the company would "outperform the market." Last week, Intel forecast its chip revenue to decline in the mid-20 per cent range for its fourth quarter and the slowdown would last into 2027.

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Nov 3 : The US Senate Commerce Committee will hold a hearing November 10 on President Donald Trump's nominee to serve on the five-member Federal Communications Commission that is considering the fate of Walt Disney's eight company-owned ABC television stations. In August, Trump nominated Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chair Brendan Carr, to serve on one of the two open seats. The FCC currently has two Republicans and one Democrat, Commissioner Anna Gomez, who some believe Trump might fire if his nominee is confirmed. The FCC historically is divided 3-2 with the party in control of the White House holding a majority. The law requires three members for a quorum. US law requires that only three of the five FCC commissioners can be from the same political party. Last month, Democratic US Senator Ron Wyden said that a 1982 law requires the FCC to have political balance at any operational size. If there are three commissioners on the FCC, only two can be from the same political party, Wyden said.

Some of those agencies are required by law to have commissioners from both parties. In April, Carr ordered an unprecedented early license review for all of Disney's ABC stations. The day before his order, Trump urged ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel. Disney's stations' license renewals were not scheduled to be considered until October 2028. Before April, the FCC had not ordered an early review in more than 50 years. Disney has sued the FCC to block an early review of the ABC licenses and a US judge has not yet issued a ruling. Carr said last week he had not made any decisions on whether to seek to revoke them. At the Senate committee hearing, Severs is likely to face questions on the FCC's oversight of Disney as well as efforts to expand wireless spectrum and attempts by Elon Musk's SpaceX company to obtain wireless spectrum in order to compete with the three major US telecom carriers. Trump has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop comedy or news programs he dislikes or which have been critical of his administration. He has pressed Carr to revoke licenses of broadcasters he finds unfair. In July, Trump called on the FCC to revoke licenses of Comcast-owned NBC and ABC for deciding not to air his remarks on election security on their broadcast channels. Broadcasters have broad First Amendment rights to make content decisions. Individual broadcast stations need FCC licenses to use public airwaves. While license revocations are exceptionally rare, critics say the prospect of losing a license can pressure broadcasters and raise concerns about government interference in editorial and programming decisions.

Nov 3 - US Senator Elizabeth Warren and four other lawmakers questioned McDonald's use of algorithmic pricing tools in a letter to CEO Chris Kempczinski, which the lawmakers shared with Reuters. The letter, dated November 2, cites a Reuters story from September 29 that found McDonald’s uses machine learning algorithms to generate what the company calls the “optimal price” recommendations for each menu item at each restaurant, based in part on an estimate of how much each store’s typical patrons are willing to pay. “We are concerned that McDonald’s may be using AI to squeeze consumers into paying higher prices, and that its AI pricing tools may facilitate collusion between franchisees who should be operating as competitors,” reads the letter, which was signed by Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, along with Democratic Representatives Greg Casar, Becca Balint, Jesus Garcia and Mary Gay Scanlon. The letter asks Kempczinski several questions, including whether the pricing tools use individual consumer data from McDonald's loyalty program, how franchisees might be encouraged to use the tools, and what antitrust review was done before the tools’ deployment. The lawmakers requested a response by November 16.

Nov 3 : Apple shares tumbled about 4 per cent on Tuesday as its first results under new CEO John Ternus showed that rising memory chip costs were denting the iPhone maker's envied margins, the latest sign of the AI boom's toll on the technology industry. Sales of smartphones, PCs and other electronics have already suffered this year from price hikes driven by soaring memory chip costs as the AI industry's data-center race absorbs supply. That even Apple, long known for its supply-chain prowess, is feeling the squeeze shows virtually no firm is spared. The warning follows Intel's bleak forecast last week on collapsing PC chip demand. "What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," Ternus said on his first earnings call as CEO.

"For the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs. And looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase." Gross margin, the share of revenue Apple keeps after production costs, slipped to 47.9 per cent in the September quarter from the June quarter, even with the boost from tariff refunds. The company expects its gross margin to shrink further to between 45 per cent and 46 per cent in the December quarter, as it also grapples with the costs of rolling out an AI-powered Siri that is central to its AI plans. To cushion the blow, Apple has been drawing on memory chips bought earlier at lower prices and has moved to lock in supplies. Its manufacturing purchase obligations, or orders placed with suppliers and contract manufacturers, increased by $33 billion to $89.7 billion as of Sept. 26, a filing showed. TERNUS' PRODUCT BLITZ Apple's drop on Tuesday also weighed on the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq. Expectations were high going into the results because Apple's restraint on AI spending had made it a refuge for investors uneasy about the AI boom's soaring costs, helping its shares gain by more than a fifth so far this year. The memory crunch comes just as Ternus rolls out a product blitz packed with Apple firsts, including its first foldable phone, iPhone Duo, and its first touchscreen MacBooks. Apple has also been raising prices to cushion the hit to profitability. That, along with strong demand for the premium iPhone 18 Pro lineup, helped it beat fourth-quarter sales estimates and forecast upbeat revenue. But some analysts warn that more price hikes risk scaring off buyers as inflation is already climbing. The CEO comments imply "Apple products are going to become even more expensive, which is not ideal at a time when the consumer is feeling the pinch from a higher cost of living," said Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell. Apple is set to lose over $170 billion in market value from its $4.94 trillion valuation, if losses hold. The stock trades at nearly 35 times expected earnings over the next 12 months, compared with 18.23 times for Alphabet and 23.43 times for Microsoft.

Nov 3 : Elon Musk’s recent super-sized pay packages at SpaceX and Tesla were centered on some eye-popping goals: creating a 1 million-person human colony on Mars, putting a million robotaxis on the road and selling a million humanoid robots. A merger combining Musk’s trillion-dollar rocket and electric vehicle firms would mean he might not ever need to meet those lofty targets to achieve his ultimate goal: control over his corporate empire. Musk said on a SpaceX earnings call last month that both companies' boards had formed special committees to discuss a potential merger. A deal could give him the voting control at Tesla that he has said he wants, without his having to hit any of the milestones in his pay plan. As for Musk’s compensation, a merger initially would likely award him only a sliver of the $1 trillion in stock from last year’s widely discussed Tesla pay package, according to a Reuters review of the plan and six executive-compensation experts. SpaceX’s board could also restructure his compensation plan after a potential Tesla deal, the experts said.

An examination of Musk’s compensation packages at both companies shows that the structure of SpaceX’s plan, which gives Musk voting power upfront before earning the stock, helps provide a shortcut to gaining control of Tesla. That makes the provocative, futuristic Mars and humanoid robot goals more of an afterthought, according to the experts who reviewed the plans for Reuters. “It’s irrelevant,” said Charles Elson, founding director of the Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware. “This package is a distraction from the real story, which is complete control.” 'AMBITIOUS STUFF' The $1 trillion Tesla compensation plan that shareholders approved for Musk last year required him to hit a series of market-capitalization and operational milestones in order to collect more stock and amass more voting control. Leading up to SpaceX’s IPO this summer, the company’s board granted Musk stock awards tied to boosting the company’s market cap, getting a million people to Mars and building massive space data centers. Unless Musk achieved the Mars and data center goals, he could not pocket the shares, according to the agreements. Importantly, though, Musk immediately got all the voting power associated with those shares, just not the economic rights. That got him to 85 per cent control over SpaceX without needing to hit any goals. Musk already had significant ownership in SpaceX before being awarded those additional voting rights. Matthew Bloomfield, an associate professor of accounting at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School, said he viewed the SpaceX plan, crafted so close to the IPO, as “just a marketing document.” “You put a bunch of ambitious stuff in there and a lot of people say, ‘Look at this big bet Elon Musk is putting on himself,’” he said. In reality, the plan is mostly about “getting a bunch of people hyped,” he said. Musk, Tesla and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment. The story at Tesla is the opposite. A flashy compensation package that awarded Musk up to $1 trillion in Tesla stock last year was designed to give him more control over the company, but only as he meets operational and market-cap goals over time. Musk has not yet achieved any of the targets in the Tesla plan. Even if he were to hit all of the goals, including increasing the company's market cap nearly eightfold, he would have only about 29 per cent of the voting power at Tesla, according to documents the board presented last year. As Tesla’s board was shopping the plan to investors last year, Musk himself said that gaining more control over Tesla was the goal, highlighting the risks of building AI-powered robots. “My fundamental concern with regard to how much voting control I have in Tesla is: If I go ahead and build this enormous robot army, can I just be ousted at some point in the future?” he said on an October 2025 Tesla earnings call. MERGER OFFERS SHORTCUT TO TESLA CONTROL A merger offers a far quicker path to getting that control. Barclays analysts estimated in a recent investor note that at the current size of each company, if SpaceX were to acquire Tesla, then Musk would own about 37 per cent of the new conglomerate but have 56 per cent of the voting power. That is because many of his SpaceX shares are in a special class that carries 10 times the voting rights of the typical shareholder. There is no such class of shares at Tesla. Musk’s SpaceX and Tesla compensation plans contemplate what would happen in the event of a merger. For Tesla, the language in the agreement is straightforward. In a “change in control” event such as an acquisition by SpaceX, Musk could receive stock payouts for meeting market-cap goals without the added requirement of an operational goal like having 1 million robotaxis in operation. The market cap would be calculated based on the stock price immediately before the merger or the value that Tesla shareholders receive from the transaction, whichever is greater. Tesla’s current market capitalization is about $1.6 trillion. That would need to grow to $2 trillion in connection with the merger for Musk to receive any stock awards under the plan. (Meeting that goal would issue him $20 billion in Tesla shares at a $2 trillion valuation, though it would be worth less because the plan only compensates Musk for stock growth after his pay plan was announced, in September 2025.) Musk could receive more if the market capitalization grew to $2.5 trillion, $3 trillion or higher after a deal, though the six compensation experts said such a premium would be unlikely. SPACEX BOARD COULD REVISE MUSK'S PLAN The SpaceX compensation plan is less specific about what happens in the event of a merger, and compensation experts said the board could significantly adjust Musk's plan after a transaction. Musk’s plan at SpaceX is divided into two parts: a series of market-cap goals, paired with a goal of setting up a colony on Mars with a million people; and another set of market-cap goals, alongside a target of building space data centers capable of “delivering 100 terawatts of compute per year.” Musk said on X earlier this year that 100 terawatts per year would be "200 times the current electricity output of Earth," and would require manufacturing satellites on the moon that would be "shot into deep space." Musk is already able to vote all the shares awarded to him in the SpaceX plan, but he cannot get any value out of them unless he achieves those goals. So even if he more than triples the value of SpaceX, and gets 500,000 people to Mars, he would not earn any of the shares, according to the plan. The shares in Musk's plan would be worth $719 billion at the highest market cap target, based on SpaceX's current shares outstanding, according to research firm Equilar. Kevin Murphy, a finance professor at USC's Marshall School of Business and an expert witness for Tesla in defending Musk’s 2018 pay package, said he thinks the board and Musk are likely to keep all the plans in place. They could simply increase the market-cap and earnings goals, and adjust the share awards, to account for the larger combined company, he said. SpaceX did something similar earlier this year when it acquired xAI and assumed Musk’s compensation plan from that firm. Though Musk’s SpaceX plan has incredibly difficult goals, four of the compensation experts said the board could likely amend the plan however it wants. With Musk already owning nearly half of SpaceX, whether he ultimately gets a million people to Mars and pockets the additional stock from his compensation plan is less important than the control, the compensation experts said. Murphy acknowledged that goals like the Mars colony are “pretty pie-in-the-sky,” but said Musk is not likely to want an easy payday upfront. “He’s an all-or-nothing kind of guy,” Murphy said. “He doesn't want a couple cookies. He wants the whole bag.”

BRUSSELS, Nov 3 : The European Commission said on Tuesday it approved the $2.5 billion acquisition by Chinese e-commerce giant JD.com of German electronics retailer Ceconomy provided it complies with the remedies offered. A person familiar with the matter had told Reuters last month the Commission, which is which is the EU competition enforcer, was set to approve the deal. The Commission was investigating the deal under the Foreign Subsidies Regulation and was evaluating whether JD.com received preferential financing, tax incentives and grants from the Chinese government that may have helped it to offer a higher price for Ceconomy.

Source: Reuters
